extra.message: User-controlled registration code (form.registration_code.data) is interpolated directly into a raw SQL string via f-string and passed to session.execute(text(...)) in validate_token(). An attacker can inject SQL such as "' OR '1'='1" to bypass registration-code validation or extract data. This allows SQL injection.

The 'search' query parameter (request.args.get('search')) is interpolated via f-string into a raw SQL fragment text(f"text like '%{search_param}%'") used in a SQLAlchemy filter. An attacker can inject SQL to read arbitrary data (e.g. ' UNION SELECT ...), bypassing the Note.user_id restriction. This allows SQL injection.

The 404 error handler builds a template with render_template_string using an f-string containing the attacker-controlled request.path. A crafted URL containing Jinja2 expressions (e.g. /{{7*7}} or {{config}} / {{''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__()}}) is evaluated server-side, leading to server-side template injection and remote code execution.

cwe: CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')

extra.message: The before_request handler deserializes the attacker-controlled 'preferences' cookie using pickle.loads(b64decode(preferences)). Pickle deserialization of untrusted data leads to arbitrary code execution on the server.

download() fetches a fully user-controlled URL with urllib.request.urlopen (called from routes/account.py:60 with form.url.data). An attacker can request internal services (http://169.254.169.254/, http://localhost:...) or local files via the file:// scheme, and the response body is base64-encoded into the user's profile_image which is later rendered back, enabling exfiltration. This is server-side request forgery; urlopen is also called without a timeout, allowing worker-exhaustion DoS.

GET /accounts/<user_id>/notes returns all notes (including private ones) for the user_id supplied in the URL without verifying it matches current_user.id. Any authenticated user can read any other user's private notes (insecure direct object reference).

cwe: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

extra.message: delete_note() fetches a Note by the note_id from the URL and deletes it with no ownership check (note.user_id vs current_user.id). Any authenticated user can delete any other user's notes by iterating IDs.
The POST /account route (update_account) lacks the @login_required decorator (unlike GET /account and /account/image), allowing unauthenticated requests to reach the account-update logic.

cwe: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function

extra.message: update_account() copies every form field except 'password' into current_user.__dict__.update(filtered_values). AccountForm includes an 'is_admin' BooleanField, so any user can submit is_admin=true to escalate themselves to administrator (mass assignment). Other unintended attributes can also be overwritten.

cwe: CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes

extra.message: User-controlled note.text is rendered with the |safe filter ({{ note.text | safe }}), bypassing Jinja2 autoescaping. Since notes created by any user are shown on the shared home feed, an attacker can store arbitrary HTML/JavaScript that executes in other users' browsers (stored XSS).

extra.message: render_table is called with safe_columns=['text'], causing user-controlled note text to be rendered without HTML escaping. This enables stored XSS when viewing the personal notes page (including other users' notes via the IDOR at /accounts/<user_id>/notes).

extra.message: The Flask secret_key is hardcoded to the predictable value "super secret key". Attackers can forge signed session cookies (e.g. impersonate any user in flask-login sessions) and sign malicious data.

A static, hardcoded registration code 'a36e990b-0024-4d55-b74a-f8d7528e1764' is seeded on every fresh install. Anyone with access to this source code can use the known code to register accounts, defeating the registration-code access control.

Default accounts are seeded with weak, publicly known passwords: user@evfa.com/'user' and admin@evfa.com/'admin' (admin). These well-known credentials allow trivial takeover of the admin account on default deployments.

The Flask application is created without any CSRF protection (no flask-wtf CSRFProtect, and all forms use plain wtforms.Form with no csrf_token). State-changing routes such as POST /account, /account/image, /notes, /notes/<id>/delete, /registration-codes and /darkmode accept cross-site requests, enabling CSRF attacks (e.g. forcing an admin to create registration codes or a victim to change their email/password).

response.set_cookie('preferences', ...) (also at line 127) sets a security-relevant cookie without Secure, HttpOnly, or SameSite attributes. Combined with the pickle deserialization of this cookie, the missing flags increase exposure to cookie theft and CSRF-based delivery of malicious pickle payloads.
